data_source: Pre-assessment medicines list; anaesthetic pre-op assessment; anaesthetic chart (technique, airway, gastric ultrasound if used).

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'GLP-1/GIP agonist: yes/no → aspiration risk (low/raised), plan' prompt to the pre-assessment and anaesthetic pre-op templates.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 patients on these drugs, same template.
close_loop: Present at anaesthetic governance and the pre-assessment team. If it works, keep the prompt and publish a one-page local guide.
evidence: [2970] 59 UK trusts, peri-operative steroid replacement: 9% overall compliance (single cycle)
[2782] Southampton peri-operative diabetes: intra-operative glucose monitoring 59% (single cycle)
pitfalls: Weight-loss injections bought privately are missing from GP lists → ask directly at pre-assessment.
Staff still stop the drug for a week → record 'stopped' separately and share the new guidance.
Definitions of 'assessment' vary → agree minimum content before cycle 1.
Few cases in cycle 1 → extend the time window, not the inclusion criteria.
pearls: Recruit a pre-assessment pharmacist to search medication lists.
Include endoscopy sedation lists; they see many of these patients.
Share the national consensus infographic with the change.
Name a consultant who owns the local guide.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from pre-assessment and anaesthetic notes

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: In adults taking an SGLT2 inhibitor (e.g. dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) who have elective surgery, what proportion omit it on both the day before and the day of the procedure?
why: SGLT2 inhibitors cause euglycaemic ketoacidosis after surgery and are now used for heart failure and kidney disease, not just diabetes. The library diabetes audit did not look at these drugs [2782].

standard.source: Association of Anaesthetists, CPOC, RCoA and partners, Elective peri-operative management of adults taking GLP-1 RAs, GIP/GLP-1 RAs and SGLT2 inhibitors: consensus statement (Anaesthesia 2025)
standard.wording: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors should be omitted the day before and the day of a procedure.

pass: Pre-assessment instruction to omit on the day before and the day of surgery, and the admission record confirms no dose was taken on either day.
population: Adults on an SGLT2 inhibitor for any indication (diabetes, heart failure, kidney disease) having elective surgery or procedures under anaesthesia or sedation.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over 1–2 months.
data_source: Pre-assessment medicines instructions; day-of-surgery admission checklist or medicines reconciliation; EPMA; ketone results if checked.

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add SGLT2 inhibitors (by drug name, all indications) to the pre-assessment electronic 'omit' list with an automatic day-before and day-of instruction letter.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at anaesthetic and diabetes governance. If it works, add sick-day rules to the discharge letter template.
evidence: [2782] Southampton peri-operative diabetes: HbA1c and ketones checked in 53% (single cycle; targeted education planned)
[2970] 59 UK trusts, peri-operative steroid replacement: 9% compliance (single cycle)
pitfalls: Heart failure patients are not flagged as 'diabetic' → search by drug name, not diagnosis.
Only day-of omission advised → check the wording of every leaflet.
Whether the day-before dose was taken is not asked → add it to the admission checklist.
Cardiologists worry about stopping → the omission is only 2 days; share the consensus.
pearls: Recruit a pharmacist to run a drug-name search.
Include day-surgery units.
Add restart advice at discharge in the same change.
Keep the drug list up to date as new SGLT2 inhibitors appear.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from pre-assessment and admission records

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: In adults on a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion during surgery and recovery, what proportion have a capillary blood glucose checked at least every hour?
why: A Southampton audit found intra-operative glucose monitoring in only 59% and recovery monitoring in 63% of patients with diabetes, with no second cycle [2782]. The 2026 consensus restates hourly checks.

standard.source: Association of Anaesthetists and Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, Peri-operative management of diabetes mellitus: consensus statement (Anaesthesia 2026)
standard.wording: Check a capillary blood glucose every hour for patients who are placed on a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion.

pass: No gap longer than 60 minutes between glucose readings from the start of anaesthesia to discharge from recovery while the insulin infusion runs.
population: Adults with diabetes on a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion at any point from induction to recovery discharge, elective or emergency.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over 1–2 months.
data_source: Anaesthetic chart and recovery chart (glucose values and times); point-of-care glucose meter download; EPMA (insulin infusion times).

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add hourly glucose prompt rows to the anaesthetic and recovery charts that appear when an insulin infusion is started, and link the glucose meters to the EPR.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at anaesthetic governance and the inpatient diabetes team. If it works, keep the prompts and add a VRII section to the theatre–ward handover.
evidence: [2782] Southampton peri-operative diabetes: intra-operative glucose monitoring 59%, recovery 63%, handover 42% (single cycle)
pitfalls: Meter readings are not transcribed → download from the meter to check.
Short cases under an hour → need only one intra-operative reading; define rules before cycle 1.
Recovery nurses unaware of VRII → include recovery staff in the change.
Few eligible patients → extend the time window.
pearls: Recruit the inpatient diabetes specialist nurse.
Ask point-of-care testing for meter data by location.
Report hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia episodes as outcomes.
Use the same gap rule in both cycles.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from charts and meter download

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: In adults having general anaesthesia with at least one PONV risk factor, what proportion receive prophylaxis with two antiemetic interventions?
why: Nausea and vomiting after surgery delays discharge and is one of the most disliked outcomes. The library has only incidental PONV data within ERAS audits [2888]; no closed-loop audit of risk-based prophylaxis exists.

standard.source: Fifth Consensus Guidelines for the Management of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting: Executive Summary (Gan et al., Anesth Analg 2026;143:497–513), Guideline 3
standard.wording: Guideline 3. Administer PONV prophylaxis using 2 interventions in adults at any risk for PONV ... Since most adult patients undergoing surgery and anesthesia will have at least one risk factor for PONV, a general multimodal approach is recommended for administering PONV prophylaxis.

pass: Two prophylactic interventions from different classes (e.g. dexamethasone plus ondansetron, or one drug plus TIVA) recorded on the anaesthetic chart.
population: Adults (18+) having general anaesthesia for elective or emergency surgery with ≥1 Apfel risk factor (female, non-smoker, history of PONV or motion sickness, postoperative opioids). Exclude patients going to ICU ventilated.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible cases from mixed day-case and inpatient lists over 2 weeks.
data_source: Electronic anaesthetic chart (antiemetics, TIVA); pre-op assessment (risk factors); recovery chart (PONV, rescue).

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a default 'PONV prophylaxis: dexamethasone + ondansetron (untick with reason)' bundle to the electronic anaesthetic chart.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: 40 consecutive eligible cases, same lists and template.
close_loop: Present at the anaesthetic department meeting with recovery PONV rates. If it works, keep the chart bundle and add PONV to the recovery quality dashboard.
evidence: [2888] Elective colorectal ERAS audit: >90% compliance with PONV prophylaxis within an ERAS pathway (single cycle)
[1341] Queen Elizabeth Birmingham surgery: antiemetic co-prescribing with opioids >75% after education and reminders
[1429] Italian orthopaedic theatres without PACU: 6 of 261 patients failed discharge criteria for nausea/vomiting (single cycle)
pitfalls: Dexamethasone avoided in diabetes → record the reason; a documented alternative counts.
Apfel score not documented → derive it from the notes and keep the same method in both cycles.
Anaesthetists resist 'recipe' anaesthesia → keep an untick-with-reason option.
PONV outcome under-recorded in recovery → add a yes/no field to the recovery chart.
pearls: Recruit the recovery sister to record PONV and rescue.
Present day-case unplanned admissions due to PONV if available.
Pharmacy can confirm drug stock in each anaesthetic room.
Run cycle 1 on the same lists you will re-audit.
effort: ~10 min per 10 cases from electronic anaesthetic and recovery charts

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: In adults who vomit or feel sick after surgery despite prophylaxis, what proportion receive their first rescue antiemetic from a different drug class to the prophylaxis?
why: Repeating the same drug (usually ondansetron) soon after prophylaxis gives little extra benefit. No library audit has measured PONV rescue choice.

standard.source: Fifth Consensus Guidelines for the Management of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting: Executive Summary (Gan et al., Anesth Analg 2026;143:497–513), Guideline 4
standard.wording: Patients should receive rescue treatment from a different pharmacological class to the prophylactic agents administered. If more than 6 hours has elapsed, administration of a second dose of a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist or butyrophenone may be considered if no alternatives are available.

pass: First rescue antiemetic (in recovery or within 24 hours on the ward) is from a class not used for prophylaxis, or a repeat 5-HT3 antagonist given more than 6 hours after the prophylactic dose.
population: Adults (18+) who received antiemetic prophylaxis during anaesthesia and then received a rescue antiemetic within 24 hours. Exclude patients in ICU.
sample: 40 consecutive patients who received rescue antiemetics, from EPMA/recovery records over 3–4 weeks.
data_source: Anaesthetic chart (prophylactic drugs and times); recovery chart and EPMA (rescue drug and time).

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Replace the generic 'ondansetron PRN' recovery and ward order set with a PONV rescue ladder that lists the drugs given in theatre and suggests a different class first (e.g. cyclizine, prochlorperazine, droperidol).
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 rescue episodes, same template.
close_loop: Present at anaesthetic governance and recovery nursing meeting. If it works, embed the rescue ladder in the post-operative order set.
evidence: [1341] Queen Elizabeth Birmingham surgery: antiemetic co-prescribing with opioids >75% (education, posters, weekly reminders)
[1429] Italian orthopaedic theatres without PACU: nausea/vomiting among causes of unmet discharge criteria (single cycle)
pitfalls: Recovery nurses only have ondansetron under a PGD → update the PGD or order set before cycle 2.
Prophylaxis not recorded clearly → use the electronic chart as the only source.
Droperidol availability varies → offer two alternatives in the ladder.
Ward and recovery rescue differ → report both settings separately.
pearls: Recruit a recovery nurse and a surgical pharmacist.
Collect second-rescue rates; they show the benefit.
Show the ladder on the recovery drug trolley.
Pair this audit with the prophylaxis audit for one presentation.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from charts and EPMA

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: For tracheal intubations outside theatres (ICU, emergency department and wards), what proportion have waveform capnography confirmation of tube placement documented?
why: Unrecognised oesophageal intubation still kills patients outside theatre. Library airway work covers an ED checklist bundle [3032] and a theatre pre-induction checklist [2968], not documented capnography confirmation in ICU and wards.

standard.source: Project for Universal Management of Airways and international airway societies (including DAS), Preventing unrecognised oesophageal intubation: consensus guideline (Anaesthesia 2022)
standard.wording: Exhaled carbon dioxide monitoring and pulse oximetry should be available and used for all episodes of airway management. ... Sustained exhaled carbon dioxide should be used to confirm alveolar ventilation following passage of a tracheal tube

pass: The intubation record documents a sustained waveform capnography trace (or end-tidal CO2 value after ≥7 breaths) as confirmation of tube placement.
population: All adult tracheal intubations and tube exchanges performed in ICU, ED, wards and cardiac arrest calls. Exclude operating theatres.
sample: 40 consecutive out-of-theatre intubations over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: ICU/ED intubation checklist or airway record; ICU notes; cardiac arrest audit forms; monitor data if archived.

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'Sustained exhaled CO2 confirmed (waveform): yes/no' line to the out-of-theatre intubation checklist and airway record.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 out-of-theatre intubations, same template.
close_loop: Present at ICU/ED airway governance and the resuscitation committee. If it works, add capnography to every emergency airway trolley check.
evidence: [3032] Australian major trauma ED: first-attempt success 88.5% → 94.6% (monthly audit, education, intubation checklist)
[2968] Swiss anaesthesia pre-induction checklist: completion 48.3% → 66.7% over five years (single audit series)
pitfalls: Capnography used but not written down → the checklist line fixes documentation; say so when presenting.
Cardiac arrest forms lack the field → update the resuscitation record too.
Low trace in cardiac arrest confuses staff → include the PUMA 'sustained CO2' criteria on the checklist.
Small numbers per month → collect from ICU, ED and arrest calls together.
pearls: Recruit an ICU airway lead and an ED consultant.
Check every emergency airway trolley has a working capnography line during weeks 5–12.
Record videolaryngoscope use at the same time.
Report any recognised oesophageal intubations anonymously.
effort: ~15 min per 10 intubations from airway records

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: After thyroid surgery, what proportion of adults have observations including wound inspection recorded at least hourly for the first 6 hours?
why: Neck haematoma after thyroidectomy can obstruct the airway within hours; half occur in the first 6 hours. Library thyroid audits cover calcium and voice outcomes [2511] [2799], not early postoperative monitoring.

standard.source: DAS, BAETS and ENT UK, Management of haematoma after thyroid surgery: consensus guidelines (Anaesthesia 2022)
standard.wording: Thus, routine patient observations should be carried out at least hourly for first 6 h postoperatively ... Minimum monitoring includes wound inspection, early warning and pain scoring, as well as awareness for more subtle signs (agitation; anxiety; difficulty in breathing; discomfort).

pass: Observations (NEWS2, pain score and wound/neck check) recorded with no gap over 60 minutes from recovery discharge until 6 hours after end of surgery.
population: Adults having hemi, total or completion thyroidectomy (and parathyroidectomy via neck incision if agreed). Exclude patients kept in ICU/HDU.
sample: All thyroid operations over the last 6 months (expect 30–50 in a DGH with a thyroid surgeon).
data_source: E-observations or paper charts (times, NEWS2, pain score); nursing notes (wound check); theatre system (end of surgery).

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'post-thyroid surgery' observation schedule to the e-observations system (hourly for 6 hours with a neck/wound check field and DESATS prompts), triggered by the procedure code.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14 onward: next 20–30 thyroid operations (low volume), same template.
close_loop: Present at ENT/endocrine surgery and anaesthetic governance. If it works, keep the schedule and add the emergency box check to the ward safety huddle.
evidence: [2511] Somerset thyroidectomy calcium management: guideline followed 100% and no readmissions after a pre-operative pack and updated guidelines
[1221] James Cook spinal surgery: 12/25 → 21/25 post-operative care domains at 100% (post-operative checklist)
pitfalls: Low volume → use 6–12 months for cycle 1 and keep collecting until 20 cases for cycle 2.
Obs recorded but no wound check → the field must be separate.
Patients moved to wards far from the nursing station → record bed location too.
Night staffing pushback → hourly obs apply only to the first 6 hours.
pearls: Recruit the ENT or endocrine ward sister.
Check for the post-thyroid emergency box at the same time.
Invite the thyroid surgeon to co-present.
Use the DAS/BAETS/ENT UK post-thyroid surgery review chart as the template.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from e-observations

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: What proportion of adults with a BMI over 40 are flagged as such on the published theatre list?
why: Airway complications are more frequent in people living with obesity and preparation depends on the team knowing in advance. Library bariatric audits cover cancellations [2748], not theatre-list flags.

standard.source: Society for Obesity and Bariatric Anaesthesia, Airway management in patients living with obesity: best practice recommendations (Anaesthesia 2025)
standard.wording: Operating theatre lists should flag patients with a BMI > 40 kg.m-2 (Grade D, strong recommendation).

pass: The final published theatre list shows BMI or an obesity flag for the patient.
population: Adults with BMI >40 kg/m2 (from pre-assessment or admission weight) on elective or emergency theatre lists, any specialty.
sample: 40 consecutive patients with BMI >40 over 4–6 weeks.
data_source: Theatre management system (published list); pre-assessment or admission record (height, weight, BMI); team brief record.

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make BMI a mandatory field when booking a case in the theatre system and display it automatically on the printed and electronic list, with a flag above 40.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 patients with BMI >40, same template.
close_loop: Present at theatre users' group. If it works, add BMI to the WHO team brief script.
evidence: [2748] Chelsea and Westminster bariatric surgery: cancellations 30.5% → 17.3% (early anaesthetic-led pre-assessment)
[3048] NHS theatres WHO checklist: team brief done in 7/8 sessions, debrief 2/8 (single cycle)
pitfalls: BMI missing for emergency cases → allow 'estimated' and record weight on admission.
Patients object to BMI on public screens → show a neutral flag icon rather than the number.
Booking clerks bypass mandatory fields → ask IT to block list publication without BMI.
Definitions change (BMI >35 vs >40) → keep 40 in both cycles.
pearls: Recruit the theatre scheduling manager.
Check emergency lists separately; they fail most.
Show a near miss (equipment not ready) to explain why.
Record team brief discussion as a second measure.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from theatre system

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: For central venous catheters inserted in theatre or intensive care, what proportion have witnessed documentation that the guidewire was removed?
why: A retained guidewire is a Never Event. Library central line audits cover timely removal [2120] and coagulation checks [2423], not guidewire documentation.

standard.source: Association of Anaesthetists guidelines: safe vascular access 2025 (Anaesthesia 2025)
standard.wording: All possible procedures should be put in place to prevent retained guidewires, including operator vigilance; guidewire counts; mandatory witnessed documentation of guidewire removal; and where available, the use of guidewire anti-retention devices.

pass: The CVC insertion record or LocSSIP checklist states the guidewire was removed and names or signs a second person as witness.
population: All non-tunnelled central venous catheters, dialysis lines and PICCs inserted by anaesthetists or intensivists in theatre, ICU or ED. Exclude tunnelled lines placed in radiology.
sample: 40 consecutive insertions over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: CVC insertion record or LocSSIP sticker in EPR; ICU line log; anaesthetic chart.

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Replace free-text line notes with a vascular access LocSSIP sticker/EPR form that has a 'Guidewire removed and shown to: ___ (signature)' box.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 insertions, same template.
close_loop: Present at ICU and anaesthetic governance and the NatSSIPs group. If it works, make the form the only way to document a line.
evidence: [2120] Surgical ICU central lines: removal alerts created 25% → 65% (step-by-step guide to the electronic alert)
[220] UHBW Stop Before You Block: 80% checked before block → full assurance at re-audit [505] (awareness work)
[508] Stockport prone ventilation safety checklist: significant assurance (single cycle)
pitfalls: Theatre lines documented on the anaesthetic chart only → accept the chart if the witness is named.
Assistants not trained to witness → brief ODPs and ICU nurses before the change.
Paper stickers run out → keep stock in every line trolley and add an EPR version.
Emergency lines out of hours are missed → audit day and night separately.
pearls: Recruit the ICU nurse educator and the theatre ODP lead.
Record ultrasound use too; it is in the same guideline.
Keep a blank form on the CVC trolley.
Present any Never Event learning nationally to show relevance.
effort: ~10 min per 10 insertions from line records

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: In adults having major elective surgery with blood cross-matched or a transfusion anticipated, what proportion have a documented pre-operative discussion about transfusion and its alternatives?
why: Valid consent for transfusion is a national requirement, yet documentation is patchy; a general surgery audit improved it after feedback [2458]. No audit has targeted major elective surgery before the day of operation.

standard.source: Association of Anaesthetists guidelines: the use of blood components and their alternatives (Anaesthesia 2025), recommendation 2
standard.wording: Where blood transfusion is anticipated, this and alternatives to transfusion should be discussed with the patient before surgery, and their consent should be documented according to local protocols.

pass: Consent form, pre-assessment or anaesthetic note documents a discussion of transfusion risks, benefits and alternatives, and the patient's decision, before the day of surgery or before induction.
population: Adults having major elective non-orthopaedic surgery (e.g. colorectal, hepatobiliary, upper GI, gynae-oncology, urology, vascular) for whom blood was cross-matched or a transfusion was judged likely.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over 4–6 weeks.
data_source: Blood bank cross-match list; surgical consent form; pre-assessment and anaesthetic pre-op notes; transfusion record.

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a transfusion section (risks, benefits, alternatives, leaflet given, decision) to the consent form or anaesthetic pre-op template for procedures with a cross-match on the maximum surgical blood ordering schedule.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the hospital transfusion committee and surgical governance. If it works, include the section in all major surgery consent forms.
evidence: [2458] District general surgery inpatients: most transfusion documentation criteria above 80% after discussion with junior doctors
[2539] East Sussex general surgery: NICE-compliant units 40.2% → 50.4% (teaching, posters)
pitfalls: Surgeons and anaesthetists each assume the other consents → agree who owns it before cycle 1.
Consent recorded only when transfusion happens → sample from the cross-match list, not the transfusion list.
Jehovah's Witness patients distort results → include them; an advance decision counts as a documented discussion.
Section left blank on the form → make it mandatory for listed procedures.
pearls: Recruit the transfusion practitioner.
Use the NHS Blood and Transplant patient leaflet.
Link the change to the maximum surgical blood ordering schedule.
Report alternatives offered; it supports patient blood management.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from consent forms and notes

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: In adults using CPAP or home non-invasive ventilation who have elective surgery, what proportion are told at pre-assessment to bring their machine on the day of surgery?
why: Patients with obstructive sleep apnoea who arrive without their CPAP face higher postoperative respiratory risk and may need HDU beds. No library audit covers this.

standard.source: Society for Obesity and Bariatric Anaesthesia, Airway management in patients living with obesity: best practice recommendations (Anaesthesia 2025)
standard.wording: Patients on CPAP/non-invasive ventilation should be instructed to bring their machine on the day of surgery (Grade C, strong recommendation).

pass: Pre-assessment record or letter documents the instruction to bring the machine, and the admission record shows it arrived.
population: Adults using CPAP, APAP or home NIV for any indication having elective surgery with an anaesthetist.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over 4–6 weeks.
data_source: Pre-assessment record and patient letters; admission checklist; recovery/ward notes (CPAP used post-op).

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add 'Uses CPAP/NIV: bring machine and mask on day of surgery' as an automatic line in the pre-assessment admission letter when CPAP is ticked.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the pre-assessment team and anaesthetic governance. If it works, add a 'CPAP on ward' check to the recovery discharge criteria.
evidence: [2748] Chelsea and Westminster bariatric surgery: cancellations 30.5% → 17.3% (early anaesthetic-led pre-assessment)
[2968] Swiss pre-induction checklist: completion 48.3% → 66.7% over five years (single audit series)
pitfalls: CPAP use not asked at pre-assessment → add a yes/no question first.
Patients forget despite instruction → add a text reminder the day before.
Wards lack power points or staff familiar with CPAP → involve the respiratory nurse.
Small numbers → extend the collection window.
pearls: Recruit the sleep or respiratory physiology team.
Include day-surgery units.
Record post-op CPAP use as an outcome.
Keep the same inclusion in both cycles.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from pre-assessment and admission records

question: What proportion of adults at high risk from sepsis (NEWS2 7 or more with suspected infection) receive IV antibiotics within 1 hour of their first ED NEWS2 score?
why: NG253 (2025, updated 2026) fixes time zero as the first ED NEWS2 score. Library sepsis audits used older bundles and screening tools [3031][2642]; none measures the 1-hour limit from the NEWS2 time stamp.

standard.wording: Give people aged 16 or over who are at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic treatment, within 1 hour of calculating the person's NEWS2 score on initial assessment in the emergency department or on ward deterioration. Only give antibiotics if they have not been given before for this episode of sepsis (see recommendations 1.7.7 and 1.7.8 on managing the condition while awaiting transfer).

pass: First IV antibiotic dose recorded as given on the drug chart within 60 minutes of the first ED NEWS2 time; or pre-hospital antibiotics already given for this episode.
population: Adults 16 or over with suspected or confirmed infection and a first ED NEWS2 of 7 or more. Exclude end-of-life care plans and patients who left before treatment.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible ED attendances over the last 2 months.
data_source: ED system or e-observations for first NEWS2 time; EPMA or drug chart for antibiotic administration time; ambulance record for pre-hospital antibiotics.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Build an automatic ED alert on the e-observations system: a NEWS2 of 7 or more with an 'infection suspected' tick opens a sepsis order set with a pre-filled antibiotic and a 60-minute countdown on the tracking board.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 consecutive eligible attendances, same template.
close_loop: Present at ED governance and the Trust deteriorating patient group. If it works, keep the alert in the e-observations build and report monthly to the sepsis lead.
evidence: [3031] paediatric severe sepsis: antibiotics within 1 hour 42% at baseline (no standard met)
[1870] delirium: compulsory electronic screen raised completion 3% → 87% (system change beats teaching)
[1358] ED VTE assessment: electronic discharge prompt 32% → 93.1% (electronic prompt)
pitfalls: Time zero recorded differently between cycles → agree in advance that time zero is the first ED NEWS2 time stamp, not triage or doctor review.
Prescription time used instead of administration time → take only the 'given' time from EPMA.
Medium-risk patients with a 3-point single parameter caused by infection are missed → add a column and decide inclusion rules before cycle 1.
Nursing staff see the audit as blame → share results by shift pattern, not by name.
Gains fade after rotation → make the alert part of the system, not a poster.
pearls: Recruit the ED sepsis nurse and the EPR analyst on day 1; they can pull NEWS2 time stamps in bulk.
Record the reason for each delay; the commonest cause tells you which fix to pick.
Use a run chart of weekly compliance, not a single percentage.
Hand the monthly report to a consultant owner before you rotate.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from e-observations and EPMA

question: What proportion of adults at high risk from sepsis who receive IV fluid in the ED are given an initial bolus of 250 ml?
why: NG253 (2025) cut the first sepsis bolus from 500 ml to 250 ml with reassessment after each bolus. Old habits and pre-printed sepsis stickers still say 500 ml. No audit of bolus volume is published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG253 recs 1.8.6 and 1.8.8 (November 2025, updated September 2026)

question: What proportion of adults at medium risk from sepsis (NEWS2 5 or 6 with suspected infection) are reviewed by an FY2-level or more senior clinician, with the venous lactate result, within 1 hour?
why: NG253 (2024, amended 2026) allows antibiotics to be deferred up to 3 hours for medium-risk patients only if a competent clinician reviews them and the lactate within 1 hour. No library audit covers the medium-risk group.

standard.wording: For people aged 16 or over with a medium risk of severe illness or death from sepsis: carry out a venous blood test, including for: blood gas, including glucose and lactate measurement ... arrange for a clinician with core competencies in the care of acutely ill patients (FY2 level or above) to review the person's condition and venous lactate results within 1 hour of the person being assessed as at medium risk. [2024, amended 2026]

pass: A timed clinical note by an FY2 or more senior clinician, mentioning the lactate result, within 60 minutes of the first NEWS2 of 5 or 6.
population: Adults 16 or over with suspected infection and a first ED NEWS2 of 5 or 6. Exclude patients who became high risk before review.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible attendances over the last 2 months.
data_source: E-observations for NEWS2 time; blood gas analyser or lab system for lactate time; ED notes for reviewer grade and time.

pass: First antibiotic dose given (IV or IO) within 60 minutes of the first recorded high risk criterion.
population: Children under 16 attending the ED with suspected sepsis and at least one NG254 high risk criterion. Exclude those given antibiotics before arrival.
sample: 30–40 consecutive eligible children over the last 3–6 months.
data_source: Paediatric ED notes and PEWS charts for criterion time; EPMA or drug chart for antibiotic time.

pass: All four values recorded in the triage or first clinician observations.
population: Children aged 0–5 years attending the ED with fever as the presenting complaint. Exclude major trauma and cardiac arrest.
sample: 50 consecutive attendances over 2 weeks.
data_source: ED system triage observations and PEWS chart.

question: What proportion of adults with a head injury and a NICE 1-hour CT risk factor have their CT head scan within 1 hour of that risk factor being identified?
why: NG232 (2023) sets a 1-hour limit for high-risk adults. The library head injury work measured neurosurgical advice time [2124] and c-spine imaging in older adults [1147]; none measures the 1-hour CT limit.

standard.wording: For people 16 and over who have sustained a head injury, do a CT head scan within 1 hour of any of these risk factors being identified: a GCS score of 12 or less on initial assessment in the emergency department; a GCS score of less than 15 at 2 hours after the injury on assessment in the emergency department; suspected open or depressed skull fracture; any sign of basal skull fracture (haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid leakage from the ear or nose, Battle's sign); post-traumatic seizure; focal neurological deficit; more than 1 episode of vomiting. [2023]

pass: CT acquisition time within 60 minutes of the first documented risk factor time.
population: Adults 16 or over with head injury and at least one rec 1.5.8 risk factor. Exclude patients already scanned elsewhere.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: ED notes for risk factor and time; PACS/RIS for request and scan times.

Split the timeline into identify → request → scan → report.
Recruit a CT superintendent radiographer early.
Show the worst delays as short case stories at governance.

question: What proportion of adults on anticoagulants with a head injury and no other CT indication have a documented CT decision with a reason?
why: NG232 (2023) changed anticoagulated head injury from 'scan all' to 'consider CT within 8 hours'. Many EDs still scan by habit or discharge without a recorded decision. No audit of this change is published in the library.

standard.wording: For people who have sustained a head injury and have no other indications for a CT head scan, but are on anticoagulant treatment (including vitamin K antagonists, direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), heparin and low molecular weight heparins) or antiplatelet treatment (excluding aspirin monotherapy), consider doing a CT head scan: within 8 hours of the injury (for example, if it is difficult to do a risk assessment or if the person might not return to the emergency department if they have signs of deterioration) or within the hour if they present more than 8 hours after the injury.

pass: Notes record a CT decision (scan or no scan) and a reason; if scanned, CT within 8 hours of injury (or within 1 hour if presenting after 8 hours).
population: Adults 16 or over on anticoagulant or non-aspirin antiplatelet therapy with head injury and no rec 1.5.8 or 1.5.9 risk factors.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 2 months.
data_source: ED notes and medication history; RIS for CT times.

question: What proportion of children with a head injury and exactly one NICE risk factor are observed for at least 4 hours from the time of injury?
why: NG232 (2023) asks for 4 hours of observation when a child has only one rec 1.5.11 risk factor. Early discharge is common in busy EDs. No library audit covers paediatric head injury observation.

standard.wording: Observe people under 16 who have sustained a head injury but have only 1 of the risk factors in recommendation 1.5.11 for a minimum of 4 hours from the time of injury. If, during observation, any of the following risk factors are identified, do a CT head scan within 1 hour: a GCS score of less than 15; further vomiting; a further episode of abnormal drowsiness. If none of these risk factors occur during observation, use clinical judgement to determine whether a longer period of observation is needed. [2023]

pass: Documented observations continue until at least 4 hours after the time of injury before discharge.
population: Children under 16 with head injury and exactly one rec 1.5.11 risk factor and no rec 1.5.10 factor.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible children over the last 3 months.
data_source: Paediatric head injury proforma, PEWS and neuro-observation chart, ED discharge time.

question: What proportion of children discharged from the ED after a head injury have a letter sent to their GP and to their health visitor or school nurse within 48 hours?

pass: GP letter sent within 48 hours of ED discharge and copied to the health visitor (under 5) or school nurse (school age).
population: Children under 16 discharged home from the ED after a head injury.
sample: 50 consecutive discharges over 2–4 weeks.
data_source: ED system discharge letter log (sent time and recipients); paediatric liaison records.

population: Adults 65 or over with head injury after a fall, discharged from the ED or observation unit. Exclude admissions.
sample: 50 consecutive discharges over 2–4 weeks.
data_source: ED notes and discharge letter; falls service referral log.

data_source: ED clerking and triage forms; liaison psychiatry notes; discharge letter.

question: What proportion of fluoroquinolone prescriptions issued from the ED have a documented reason why first-line antibiotics were inappropriate?

question: What proportion of adults with cirrhosis and ascites on long-term antibiotic prophylaxis for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis meet a NICE indication for it?

question: What proportion of adults treated for community-acquired pneumonia have antibiotics stopped at 5 days, or a documented reason to continue?
why: Five-day courses are the NICE default, reaffirmed in the 2025 pneumonia guideline. Library stewardship audits focused on surgical courses [2780, 2868] and review dates [2489]; no medical CAP duration audit is in the library.

sample: 40 consecutive CAP discharges over the last 6 weeks.
data_source: Coding for cases; e-prescribing for start and stop dates; discharge prescription; observations chart for day 5 stability; microbiology results.

close_loop: Present at the rheumatology department meeting and to the NEIAA lead. If it works, make the 4-weekly slot the default pathway for all active RA.
evidence: [2895] high-cost DMARDs: DAS28 documented 80% but at least 6-monthly in 7%
[2927] RA service audit: DAS28 documented 74.4%
[2919] GCA: baseline HbA1c 53% → 93% (dedicated clinic)
pitfalls: Follow-up takes 6 months → start cycle 1 retrospectively and accept a 3-month window in cycle 2.
Joint counts done but DAS28 not calculated → count only documented scores.
Clinic capacity limits → use nurse telephone reviews with patient-reported joint counts where validated locally.
Definition of 'monthly' varies → fix the 5-week tolerance before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the rheumatology specialist nurse team early; they will deliver the slots.
Use NEIAA data to find new active cases.
Put DAS28 in the letter header so it is easy to find.
Track time to remission as the headline outcome.
effort: ~30 min per 10 patients from clinic letters and results

question: What proportion of adult medical inpatients with a positive blood culture have their antibiotic reviewed within 24 hours of the sensitivity result?
why: De-escalation after culture results is a core stewardship step. Library antibiotic audits measured guideline choice and review dates [1896, 2489, 1994]; none measured action on blood culture results.

standard.wording: When the source of infection is confirmed or microbiological results are available: review the choice of antibiotic(s) and change the antibiotic(s) according to results, using a narrower-spectrum antibiotic, if appropriate. [2024]

pass: Within 24 hours of the sensitivity report, a documented review with the antibiotic narrowed, changed to match sensitivities, or continued with a stated reason.
population: Adult medical inpatients with a clinically significant positive blood culture and sensitivities. Exclude contaminants (as judged by microbiology), deaths before the result and end-of-life care.
sample: 40 consecutive significant positive blood cultures over the last 2 months.
data_source: Microbiology system for culture and sensitivity report times; e-prescribing for antibiotic changes; EPR notes for review.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'blood culture result reviewed: action' task in the EPR that fires to the responsible team when sensitivities are released.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 significant positive blood cultures, same template.
close_loop: Present at the antimicrobial stewardship committee. If it works, keep the task and report time-to-review monthly.
evidence: [1896] older people: Microguide compliance 53% → 83% (microbiology ward rounds, IT access, education)
[2489] surgical antibiotics: stop/review date 56% → 61.1% (email and posters)
[2994] paediatric empiric prescribing: indication and compliance 30% → 100% (weekly feedback, handover discussion, app)
pitfalls: Microbiology phones results but notes are blank → accept a documented phone call with action.
Contaminants inflate numbers → use microbiology's significance call.
Weekend results wait until Monday → report weekday and weekend separately.
Task ignored → route it to the ward pharmacist as well.
pearls: Recruit a microbiology consultant and the antimicrobial pharmacist.
Pull report times straight from the lab system.
Present bug–drug mismatches as safety events.
Pair with an IV-to-oral switch prompt.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from microbiology and e-prescribing

question: What proportion of adult smokers admitted to medical wards who accept nicotine replacement therapy have it prescribed within 12 hours of admission?
why: Delayed NRT drives early self-discharge and withdrawal. Library NRT audits are almost all in mental health [3451, 3148] or surgery and trauma [2371, 1336], where NRT was prescribed in 29–33%; no acute medicine audit is in the library.

standard.wording: 1.14.10 Offer and arrange or supply prescriptions of stop-smoking options (see the sections on stop-smoking interventions and stop-smoking pharmacotherapies in acute and mental health services). [2013, amended 2021] 1.14.15 If stop-smoking pharmacotherapy is accepted, make sure it is provided immediately. [2013]

pass: Smoking status recorded at clerking and, for smokers not declining, NRT prescribed within 12 hours of arrival with a first dose administered.
population: Adults admitted to acute medical wards who are current smokers. Exclude patients unable to take NRT (e.g. unconscious) and end-of-life care.
sample: 40 consecutive smokers admitted via AMU over the last 3–4 weeks.
data_source: EPR clerking for smoking status; e-prescribing for NRT prescription and administration times; tobacco dependence team referrals.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add an opt-out NRT order set to the AMU clerking template: smokers get combination NRT pre-selected unless the clerking doctor declines it.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 smokers admitted via AMU, same template.
close_loop: Present at acute medicine governance with the tobacco dependence team. If it works, extend the order set to all admission routes.
evidence: [2371] emergency surgery: NRT prescribed in 29% of smokers (structured teaching)
[1336] trauma: NRT 33.3% of smokers (education campaign)
[2538] day surgery: correct medicines 25% → 83% (pre-populated EPR order set)
pitfalls: Smoking status missing → count missing status as a fail and report it separately.
Patients vaping instead → record e-cigarette use and do not fail if the patient declines NRT.
NRT prescribed but not stocked on the ward → check ward stock lists first.
Opt-out order set seen as coercive → keep a one-click decline.
pearls: Recruit the tobacco dependence (CURE-type) team; they gain referrals.
Stock combination NRT on AMU.
Tell patients about ward vaping and smoking rules at clerking.
Report self-discharge rates among smokers as an outcome.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPR

question: What proportion of adults with diabetes admitted to medical wards have a documented foot risk assessment within 24 hours of admission?
why: Hospital-acquired foot ulcers are a NaDIA harm measure and heel ulcers start within days. Library diabetic foot audits were surgical and vascular [2388, 2386, 2479]; none audited admission foot checks on medical wards.

standard.wording: 1.3.3 For adults with diabetes, assess their risk of developing a diabetic foot problem at the following times: When diabetes is diagnosed, and at least annually thereafter (see the recommendation on carrying out reassessments at intervals, depending on the person's risk of developing a diabetic foot problem). If any foot problems arise. On any admission to hospital, and if there is any change in their status while they are in hospital. [2015] 1.3.4 When examining the feet of a person with diabetes, remove their shoes, socks, bandages and dressings, and examine both feet for evidence of the following risk factors: neuropathy (use a 10 g monofilament as part of a foot sensory examination); limb ischaemia (see the NICE guideline on peripheral arterial disease); ulceration; callus; infection and/or inflammation; deformity; gangrene

pass: Both feet examined with a risk category (low/moderate/high/active) documented within 24 hours of admission; moderate/high risk patients have heel offloading documented.
population: Adults with known diabetes admitted to medical wards for ≥24 hours. Exclude patients admitted primarily with an active diabetic foot problem (on a separate pathway) and end-of-life care.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with diabetes admitted to medical wards over the last 3–4 weeks.
data_source: Diabetes inpatient team list or EPR diabetes flag for cases; nursing admission assessment and medical clerking for foot check; pressure-area records for offloading.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add the NaDIA-style foot risk check (both feet, monofilament, pulses, risk category) as a mandatory item in the nursing admission assessment for patients with a diabetes flag, linked to heel offloading.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 adults with diabetes admitted to medical wards, same template.
close_loop: Present at the diabetes inpatient group and nursing quality meeting. If it works, keep the mandatory item and report hospital-acquired foot lesions to NaDIA-Harms.
evidence: [2479] vascular inpatients with diabetes: HbA1c re-checks 25% → 86% (education)
[1847] postural hypotension: lying and standing BP 28% → 96% (sticker plus teaching)
[1813] rehabilitation: 4AT on admission 0% → 92% (proforma with sticker and champions)
pitfalls: Foot check documented as 'feet OK' without detail → require a risk category.
Monofilaments not available → check ward stock before cycle 1.
Nurses and doctors each assume the other did it → name the nursing admission assessment as the place.
Gains fade as staff rotate → add the item to the nursing admission audit run monthly.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes inpatient specialist nurse and a podiatrist.
Keep monofilaments on each ward's observation trolley.
Link 'moderate/high risk' to automatic heel offloading and podiatry referral.
Report hospital-acquired foot lesions as the outcome that managers watch.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from nursing records

question: What proportion of adults treated for diabetic ketoacidosis have their usual long-acting insulin continued, or started if newly diagnosed, while on the fixed-rate insulin infusion?
why: Stopping basal insulin during DKA causes rebound ketosis when the infusion stops. A library audit found appropriate long-acting insulin on IV insulin in 45% of surgical patients [2782]; no DKA audit of basal insulin is in the library.

standard.source: JBDS-IP 02 The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (revised March 2023), p15 and key recommendations
standard.wording: In those already on long acting basal insulin, it should continue to be prescribed at their usual dose. In those newly diagnosed, then a long acting basal insulin should be commenced, at a dose of 0.25 units/Kg subcutaneously once daily. ... 4. Subcutaneous long-acting analogue/human insulin should be continued

pass: Long-acting insulin prescribed at the usual dose (or 0.25 units/kg if new) and given at the next due time while the FRIII runs, with no missed dose.
population: Adults (≥18) treated with a FRIII for DKA. Exclude patients managed in critical care on a different protocol and those on insulin pumps without basal injections.
sample: 30–40 consecutive DKA episodes over the last 6–12 months.
data_source: Diabetes team DKA list or coding for cases; e-prescribing/drug chart for basal insulin prescriptions and administrations; FRIII chart for start/stop times.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Build the basal insulin line into the DKA e-prescribing order set as a required field ('continue usual basal: name/dose' or '0.25 units/kg if new').
reaudit: Wk 13–14 onward: next 30 DKA episodes (prospective collection may be needed), same template.
close_loop: Present at the diabetes and acute medicine governance meeting. If it works, keep the order set and add basal insulin to the diabetes team's DKA review checklist.
evidence: [2782] perioperative diabetes: appropriate long-acting insulin on VRI 45%
[925] ward insulin prescribing errors (drug chart redesign)
[2538] day surgery: correct medicines 25% → 83% (pre-populated EPR order set)
pitfalls: DKA episodes are few → use a 12-month window and prospective capture.
Pump users counted wrongly → exclude or record separately.
Basal dose prescribed but omitted by nursing → record administration, not just prescription.
ED starts DKA before the ward → check ED drug charts too.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes inpatient specialist nurse; they see every DKA.
Put the basal line at the top of the DKA order set.
Report rebound ketosis or readmission as outcomes.
Add a 'basal insulin given?' question to the DKA nursing care plan.
effort: ~20 min per 10 episodes from e-prescribing

question: What proportion of adult inpatients with a capillary glucose below 4.0 mmol/L have a repeat glucose check within 15 minutes of treatment?
why: Unconfirmed recovery after hypoglycaemia leads to recurrent and severe episodes. Library work showed milder episodes preceded severe ones [1128] and delayed treatment [926]; no audit of the recheck step is in the library.

standard.source: JBDS-IP 01 The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus (revised January 2023), p11 step 4
standard.wording: 4. Repeat capillary blood glucose measurement 10-15 minutes later. If it is still less than 4.0mmol/L, repeat step 3 (no more than 3 treatments in total). If it is above 4.0mmol/L then go to step 7.

pass: A repeat capillary glucose recorded within 20 minutes of the first low reading (15 minutes after treatment, plus 5 minutes allowed because treatment time is rarely recorded).
population: Adult inpatients with diabetes on medical wards with a capillary glucose <4.0 mmol/L. Include one episode per patient (the first in the audit window). Exclude critical care.
sample: 40 consecutive hypoglycaemia episodes (one per patient) over the last 2–4 weeks.
data_source: Networked glucose meter data (time-stamped readings) for cases and recheck times; drug chart/nursing notes for treatment given.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Configure networked glucose meters to prompt 'Recheck in 10–15 minutes' after any reading <4.0 mmol/L, and place hypo boxes with a timer card on each ward.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 episodes from meter data, same template.
close_loop: Present at the diabetes inpatient safety group and nursing quality meeting. If it works, keep the meter prompt and add recheck compliance to the diabetes ward dashboard.
evidence: [1128] inpatient hypoglycaemia: over 600 events a year; milder episodes preceded severe ones (ward dashboard and after-action reviews)
[926] ward hypoglycaemia: treatment delayed (hypo boxes)
[1804] delirium sticker: use fell from 57% to 0% by week 6 (stickers alone fade)
pitfalls: Meters not networked → use paper glucose charts and accept lower precision.
Reading repeated on another meter → search by patient, not meter.
Nurses treat but record late → allow a 5-minute tolerance and state it.
Prompt ignored → pair with hypo box refresh and ward feedback.
pearls: Recruit the point-of-care testing manager; they can export meter data in minutes.
Recruit a ward nurse champion on each ward.
Report recurrent hypos within 24 hours as the outcome.
Share weekly ward-level recheck rates on the diabetes dashboard.
effort: ~10 min per 10 episodes from meter data

question: What proportion of adult inpatients with known diabetes started on glucocorticoids have capillary glucose checked four times a day?
why: Steroid hyperglycaemia is common in medical inpatients (COPD, cancer, inflammatory disease). Library audits covered screening in giant cell arteritis clinics [2919, 2945]; none audited inpatient monitoring.

standard.source: JBDS-IP 08 Management of Hyperglycaemia and Steroid (Glucocorticoid) Therapy (revised January 2023), Table 1, p9
standard.wording: Known diagnosis of diabetes: Reassess glucose control and current therapy. Set target blood glucose e.g. 6-10mmol/L. Check CBG 4 times a day and use this flowchart to adjust diabetes medication accordingly. In Type 1 diabetes also check daily for ketones if CBG >12mmol/L. Aim for 6-10mmol/L (acceptable range 6-12mmol/L).

pass: At least 4 capillary glucose readings on each of the first 3 full days of steroid therapy (or until discharge), and diabetes treatment adjusted if CBG >12 mmol/L twice in 24 hours.
population: Adult medical inpatients with known diabetes newly started on oral or IV glucocorticoid at a dose equivalent to prednisolone ≥10 mg. Exclude critical care and end-of-life care.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible inpatients over the last 4–6 weeks.
data_source: E-prescribing report of new steroid prescriptions cross-matched with diabetes flag; networked glucose meter data; drug chart for diabetes treatment changes.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Link a steroid prescription in a patient with a diabetes flag to an automatic 'CBG four times daily' monitoring order and a pop-up link to the JBDS steroid flowchart.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 eligible inpatients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the diabetes inpatient group and medicines safety committee. If it works, keep the linked order and extend to people without diabetes on high-dose steroids.
evidence: [2919] GCA: baseline HbA1c 53% → 93% and counselling 12% → 30% (regional presentation, dedicated clinic)
[2945] GCA: follow-up HbA1c 78% but joint rheumatology screening 37%
[2219] emergency surgery: dose-adjustment prompts 29/36 → 37/38 correct (drug chart checkboxes)
pitfalls: Once-daily morning steroid peaks late → check that the afternoon/evening readings are included.
Meter data not linked to patients → use paper charts for cycle 1.
Short courses (<3 days) → audit days on steroid only.
Pop-up fatigue → make it a monitoring order, not an alert.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes specialist nurse and the e-prescribing pharmacist.
Use the COPD and oncology wards, where volume is high.
Teach the 'afternoon peak' in one slide.
Report hyperglycaemia >12 mmol/L days as the outcome.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from e-prescribing and meter data

question: What proportion of adults treated with insulin-glucose for hyperkalaemia have capillary glucose monitored for at least 6 hours afterwards?
why: Insulin-glucose often causes hypoglycaemia, sometimes hours after treatment. The only library potassium audit covered guideline and lab protocols [152]; no audit of post-treatment glucose monitoring is in the library.

standard.source: UK Kidney Association (Renal Association) Clinical Practice Guideline: Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults (2020, v2 July 2022), Guideline 17.2
standard.wording: We recommend that the blood glucose concentration is monitored at regular intervals (0, 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, 360, 480 and 720 minutes) up to 12 hours after administration of insulin-glucose infusion in all patients with hyperkalaemia. (1C)

pass: Glucose recorded before treatment and at least at 30, 60, 120, 240 and 360 minutes (±15 minutes) after insulin-glucose. Full compliance to 12 hours reported as a secondary measure.
population: Adults given IV insulin-glucose for hyperkalaemia in ED, AMU or medical wards. Exclude patients in DKA on a FRIII and critical care.
sample: 40 consecutive insulin-glucose treatments over the last 6–8 weeks.
data_source: E-prescribing (insulin-glucose for hyperkalaemia) or ED records for cases; networked glucose meters and blood gas records for glucose readings; drug chart for timings.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a hyperkalaemia insulin-glucose order set that schedules glucose checks (0, 30, 60, 120, 240, 360 min, then to 12 h) as timed nursing tasks and adds 10% glucose if pre-treatment glucose is <7 mmol/L.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 insulin-glucose treatments, same template.
close_loop: Present at the renal and acute medicine governance meeting and the medicines safety committee. If it works, keep the order set and report hypoglycaemia after insulin-glucose on the safety dashboard.
evidence: [152] potassium disturbance: poor compliance → 100% on re-audit (guideline and lab protocol)
[2538] day surgery: correct medicines 25% → 83% (pre-populated EPR order set)
[1128] inpatient hypoglycaemia: ward dashboard and after-action reviews
pitfalls: Readings spread across blood gases and meters → search both sources.
Patients move from ED to AMU mid-monitoring → follow the patient, not the ward.
Strict time windows fail good care → state the ±15 minute tolerance before cycle 1.
Order set used but tasks not done → record completed readings, not scheduled ones.
pearls: Recruit the renal pharmacist and an ED nurse lead.
Put a printed timer card in the hyperkalaemia treatment pack.
Report hypoglycaemia rates to motivate staff.
Align with the local hyperkalaemia guideline so there is one document.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from meter data and ED records

area: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
question: Do adults with a suspected TIA receive aspirin 300 mg at first contact in the emergency department or acute medical unit?
why: TIA audits have measured imaging and time to specialist review [1900], [1945], but not whether aspirin is started at the first hospital contact. Delay before the TIA clinic leaves the highest-risk days untreated.

standard.wording: Offer aspirin (300 mg daily), unless contraindicated, to people who have had a suspected TIA, to be started immediately.

pass: Aspirin 300 mg (or a documented alternative antiplatelet if allergic or intolerant) given before leaving ED/AMU or within 4 hours of first hospital assessment, or a contraindication documented.
population: Adults (16+) with a working diagnosis of suspected TIA in ED or AMU. Exclude: symptoms still present at assessment (treated as stroke), already on an anticoagulant, intracranial bleed on imaging.
sample: 40 consecutive adults referred to the TIA clinic from ED/AMU over the last 3 months.
data_source: TIA clinic referral list; ED/AMU clerking; electronic prescribing and administration record (EPMA) or drug chart for dose and time given.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately
ED/AMU arrival or first clinician review
Loading dose given, not just prescribed

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'aspirin 300 mg given or contraindication' tick box to the electronic TIA clinic referral form, so the referral cannot be sent without it.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 consecutive referrals, same template.
close_loop: Present at the stroke/TIA governance meeting and ED clinical meeting. If it works, keep the referral field permanently and add it to the ED TIA pathway card.
evidence: [1900] Galway TIA pathway: patients managed within 24 hours 28.2% → 35.7% (new ambulatory pathway via AMU)
[1945] St Vincent's AMU: TIA investigations audited (CT 100%, carotid Doppler 89%); aspirin timing not measured (single cycle)
[1861] Beaumont stroke unit: antiplatelet duration on discharge letters 82% documented (single cycle, education recommended)

'Prescribed' confused with 'given' → count only a signed administration entry.
Patients already on aspirin 75 mg are marked as passes → agree before cycle 1 that a 300 mg loading dose is still expected unless the specialist says otherwise.
Stroke mimic diagnosed later → keep them in; the standard applies to suspected TIA.
pearls: Recruit the TIA clinic nurse; they already see every referral and can flag missing doses daily.
Agree the 4-hour window with the stroke lead before cycle 1 and keep it fixed.
Ask the EPR team for a report of TIA referrals with aspirin administration times to cut collection time.
Put the result on the ED safety huddle board for a month after the change.
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from EPR and EPMA

area: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
question: How many adults with a suspected TIA have a CT brain scan without a documented suspicion of an alternative diagnosis?
why: Most TIA audits report CT rates of 89–100% [1900], [1945], yet NICE advises against routine CT in suspected TIA. No closed-loop audit of unnecessary CT in TIA has been published in the library.

standard.wording: Do not offer CT brain scanning to people with a suspected TIA unless there is clinical suspicion of an alternative diagnosis that CT could detect.

pass: Either no CT brain before specialist assessment, or a CT request that states a specific alternative diagnosis CT could detect (for example subdural haematoma, tumour, head injury).
population: Adults (16+) with suspected TIA assessed in ED/AMU. Exclude: ongoing deficit (suspected stroke), anticoagulated patients with head injury, CT done for another indication (for example trauma).
sample: 40 consecutive adults with suspected TIA over the last 3 months.
data_source: TIA clinic referral list; radiology information system (RIS) for CT requests and request wording; ED/AMU notes.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately
Copy the clinical indication from RIS

change: Add a mandatory 'alternative diagnosis suspected' drop-down to the CT head request for suspected TIA in the radiology ordering system, with a note that routine CT is not needed.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 consecutive suspected TIA patients, same template.
close_loop: Present with radiology and ED at the imaging governance meeting. If it works, keep the request field and add the rule to the ED TIA pathway.

[1945] St Vincent's AMU: 100% had CT brain on admission (single cycle)
[1147] Stoke Mandeville ED: imaging rules shared by posters and teaching; documented examination unchanged at 16% (education only)

Add the rule to the junior doctor induction handbook for the next rotation.

area: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
question: Do adults with a warfarin-related intracerebral haemorrhage receive both prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K?
why: Anticoagulant reversal in ICH is reported only as a side finding in a mortality review [1858]; warfarin audits in older people focus on prescribing [1824]. No audit of reversal completeness in ICH is in the library.

standard.wording: Return clotting levels to normal as soon as possible in people with a primary intracerebral haemorrhage who were receiving warfarin before their stroke (and have elevated international normalised ratio). Do this by reversing the effects of the warfarin using a combination of prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K.

pass: Both PCC and intravenous vitamin K given, with PCC given within 90 minutes of the diagnostic CT (local timing standard), unless a documented decision for palliation only.
population: Adults with primary ICH on CT who were taking warfarin with INR above the therapeutic lower limit. Exclude: traumatic haemorrhage, DOAC users (audit separately), documented comfort-care-only decision before CT.
sample: All eligible patients over the last 24 months (expect 15–30 in a district general hospital), or SSNAP extract of ICH on anticoagulants.
data_source: SSNAP extract or stroke register (ICH on anticoagulant); PACS for CT time; laboratory system for INR; blood bank issue log for PCC; EPMA for vitamin K route and time.

Time of first CT showing ICH
From blood bank issue and administration record
Oral or subcutaneous counts as no

change: Store a pre-labelled 'ICH warfarin reversal pack' (PCC dosing chart, vitamin K 10 mg IV, INR request) in ED resus, triggered by the stroke CT result.

reaudit: At 6 months: all eligible cases since the change, same template (small numbers expected).
close_loop: Present at the stroke and haematology/transfusion committee. If it works, embed the pack in the ED ICH protocol and review each case at stroke morbidity meetings.

[1824] Queens Medical Centre older people wards: warfarin correctly continued 18% → 32% (education only)
[1951] Mater Dublin: ICH blood pressure protocol introduced; protocol violations in 66.6% (system change)

PCC given but not recorded in EPMA → cross-check the blood bank issue log.
Haematology and ED disagree on PCC dose → agree the dosing chart with haematology before the change.
Patients moved to a neurosurgical centre → collect data from the transfer letter and the receiving hospital.

Agree the 90-minute local timing standard with the stroke lead before cycle 1.
Add the reversal pack check to the monthly ED resus trolley checklist.
Extend to DOAC reversal once the warfarin loop is closed.

area: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
question: In adults with acute intracerebral haemorrhage eligible for rapid blood pressure lowering, is systolic pressure brought to 140 mmHg or lower without a fall of more than 60 mmHg in the first hour?
why: Only one closed loop exists, and it found protocol violations in two-thirds of cases after a protocol was introduced [1951]; a mortality review found target reached at 2 hours in 3 of 8 [1858]. The 2022 NICE update added a safety ceiling on the size of the drop.

standard.wording: When rapidly lowering blood pressure in people with acute intracerebral haemorrhage, aim to reach a systolic blood pressure of 140 mmHg or lower while ensuring that the magnitude drop does not exceed 60 mmHg within 1 hour of starting treatment.

pass: Systolic BP 140 mmHg or lower reached during the first 6 hours of treatment, with no reading in the first hour of treatment more than 60 mmHg below the pre-treatment systolic.
population: Adults with spontaneous ICH presenting within 6 hours of onset with systolic 150–220 mmHg (NICE rec 1.5.4). Exclude the NICE rec 1.5.7 groups: structural cause, GCS below 6, early neurosurgery, massive haematoma with poor prognosis.
sample: All eligible patients over the last 12 months (expect 30–40), or SSNAP extract.
data_source: SSNAP extract for onset and arrival; ED and stroke unit observation charts or electronic observations for BP readings; EPMA for antihypertensive start time.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately
Target reached and no drop over 60 mmHg

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: Among detained patients who did not understand their rights at the first explanation, what proportion had their rights explained again within 7 days?

standard.source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 4.28
standard.wording: Those with responsibility for patient care should ensure that patients are reminded from time to time of their rights and the effects of the Act. It may be necessary to give the same information on a number of different occasions or in different formats and to check regularly that the patient has fully understood it. Information given to a patient who is unwell may need to be repeated when their condition has improved.

pass: A further section 132 explanation (with understanding recorded) is documented within 7 days of the first explanation that was recorded as not understood, declined or not possible.

data_source: Mental Health Act office register; section 132 rights forms; nursing notes

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make the electronic section 132 form create an automatic 'repeat rights due' task at 7 days whenever the outcome is anything other than 'fully understood'.
reaudit: Wk 13–14, 40 eligible detentions, same template
close_loop: Present to the Mental Health Act governance committee and hospital managers; if it works, keep the automated task and add it to the Mental Health Act office monthly report.
evidence: [3073] High-dependency rehabilitation unit: Mental Health Act documentation compliance 77% → 98% (medication management committee, PDSA cycles, nurse self-audit)

[3119] Derby: detention justification poorly documented (single cycle)

Nurses see it as an administrative task → show the Code wording and the Care Quality Commission focus on rights.

Hand the monthly report to the Mental Health Act office manager.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients

question: What proportion of infants admitted with bronchiolitis receive none of the treatments NICE advises against (antibiotics, salbutamol, nebulised adrenaline, hypertonic saline, ipratropium, montelukast or steroids)?

[2015]

population: Children under 2 years admitted with a primary diagnosis of bronchiolitis. Exclude PICU transfers and those with a documented alternative diagnosis (viral-induced wheeze, pneumonia).
sample: 40 consecutive admissions this bronchiolitis season.
data_source: Drug chart / EPMA administration records; admission and ward-round notes for indication.

question: What proportion of children and young people treated for diabetic ketoacidosis have their intravenous insulin infusion started 1 to 2 hours after intravenous fluids began?
why: Starting insulin too early is linked with cerebral oedema; NICE sets a 1–2 hour gap and no insulin bolus. The only DKA entry in the library tests junior doctor knowledge [2207]; no audit of actual DKA fluid and insulin timing in children has been published.

standard.wording: Start an intravenous insulin infusion 1 to 2 hours after beginning intravenous fluid therapy in children and young people with DKA. If a child or young person with DKA is using an insulin pump, disconnect the pump when starting intravenous insulin therapy. [2015] ... When treating DKA with intravenous insulin in children and young people, use a soluble insulin infusion at a dosage between 0.05 units/kg/hour and 0.1 units/kg/hour. Do not give bolus doses of intravenous insulin. [2015]

pass: Insulin infusion start time is 60–120 minutes after the first IV fluid start time, at 0.05–0.1 units/kg/hour, with no IV insulin bolus.
population: Children and young people under 18 treated with IV fluids and IV insulin for DKA (pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L with ketones). Exclude those transferred in after insulin was started elsewhere.
sample: All eligible episodes over the last 24 months (typically 20–40 in a district general hospital).
data_source: DKA integrated care pathway/fluid chart for fluid start time; EPMA or infusion chart for insulin start time and rate; blood gas record for severity.

question: What proportion of children and young people recovering from diabetic ketoacidosis receive their first subcutaneous insulin dose at least 30 minutes before the intravenous insulin is stopped?
why: Stopping IV insulin before subcutaneous insulin is working causes rebound ketosis and longer stays. No audit of the DKA transition step in children has been published in the library.

standard.wording: Start subcutaneous insulin in a child or young person with DKA at least 30 minutes before stopping intravenous insulin. [2015] ... For a child or young person with DKA who is using an insulin pump, restart the pump at least 60 minutes before stopping intravenous insulin. Change the insulin cartridge and infusion set and insert the cannula into a new subcutaneous site. [2015]

pass: Subcutaneous injection given ≥30 minutes (or pump restarted ≥60 minutes) before the IV insulin stop time.
population: Children and young people under 18 treated with IV insulin for DKA who transferred to subcutaneous insulin or pump in hospital. Exclude transfers out before transition.
sample: All eligible episodes over the last 24 months.
data_source: EPMA/insulin infusion chart (stop time), subcutaneous insulin administration record, pump documentation in nursing notes.

sample: 40 consecutive courses over the last 2 months.

question: What proportion of babies started on antibiotics for risk factors or possible early-onset infection have antibiotics stopped at 36 hours when the NICE stopping criteria are met?
why: Unneeded courses keep mothers and babies in hospital and drive resistance. Neonatal antibiotic audits in the library cover NEC regimens and drug levels [3005][2983]; none measure stopping at 36 hours.

standard.wording: For babies who are being treated with intravenous antibiotics because of risk factors for early-onset infection or clinical indicators of possible infection, stop antibiotics at 36 hours if: the blood culture is negative and the initial clinical suspicion of infection was not strong and the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no clinical indicators of possible infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset infection) and the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring. [2012, amended 2026]

pass: In babies meeting all four stopping criteria, the last antibiotic dose is given within 36 hours (allow up to 40 hours) of the first dose.
population: Babies started on IV antibiotics within 72 hours of birth for suspected early-onset infection. Exclude positive blood cultures, strong initial suspicion documented, and babies with ongoing clinical indicators at 36 hours.
sample: 50 consecutive courses over the last 3 months (expect 30–40 to meet stopping criteria).
data_source: EPMA for dose times; microbiology system for culture result time; neonatal EPR for clinical review and CRP.

reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 50 consecutive courses, same template.

CRP repeat taken late → record CRP timing as a secondary item.
Seniors override the stop date → reasons are captured; review them at the stewardship meeting.
